ON: Workplace Explorer
What actually happens on a first day, what to bring, and the three things worth asking before lunch.
Write the first-day plan you would want, then run somebody else through theirs.
A job description is a negotiating document; the role is what you are held to. Learning to read the gap.
State your own role in two sentences and check it against your manager.
Who signs off what, who is consulted, and who only needs telling. The map nobody hands you.
Draw the decision map for one real task and confirm it with two colleagues.
The five systems that gate the work, and getting access before the access is urgent.
List every system your first task needs and show a working login for each.
Questions that make you look careful rather than lost, and when to batch them.
Ask three prepared questions in one sitting and record the answers usefully.
What competence looks like at ninety days, described before you get there rather than after.
Write your own ninety-day expectations and have them corrected by somebody senior.
Probation measures reliability far more than brilliance, and the evidence is mostly ordinary.
Keep a two-week record of commitments made and commitments kept.
A working relationship is built from predictable updates, not from being liked.
Run one structured check-in with an agenda you wrote.
The documented process and the real process differ. Finding the person who knows the second.
Document one real process as actually performed and have it verified.
When the work is materially different from what was advertised, and what to do about it early.
Write the comparison, name what changed, and identify who can address it.
SK: Practitioner of the Trade
Identifying the one capability the role genuinely rests on, underneath the task list.
Name it, defend the choice, and show how you would measure improvement in it.
Deliberate practice inside paid work, without pretending it is not happening.
Design a practice loop inside a real task and run it for two weeks.
Knowledge leaves with people. Extracting it before the last day, not on it.
Run a handover interview and produce something a successor could use.
Writing something down is a skill with technique, and it is the cheapest leverage available.
Document a task so a stranger completes it correctly without asking you.
The avoided task is usually the one where the gap is largest. Approaching it deliberately.
Pick the avoided thing, break it into three steps, and complete the first.
Employer-funded qualifications exist, are underused, and have a process with a deadline.
Find one you are eligible for, identify the approver, and draft the request.
Which of your skills you keep when the employer changes, and which evaporate at the door.
Sort your current skills into the two lists and justify each placement.
Automation changes the shape of a task before it removes it. Reading the change early.
Describe one task in your work that has changed shape, and what it demands now.
Teaching is the fastest way to find the holes in what you just learned.
Teach one thing to a colleague and record where their questions found gaps.
Evidence of competence that lives with you rather than in an employer system.
Assemble a portfolio entry you could show after leaving, with nothing confidential in it.
SF: Safety Practitioner
Every safety rule encodes an incident. Reading the rule back to the harm it prevents.
Take three rules where you work and state the harm each one is protecting against.
The right to stop unsafe work, where it comes from, and how to use it without theatre.
Rehearse the stop-work sentence and identify who you say it to.
Reporting routes, what protection exists, and the difference between a report and a complaint.
Identify the route where you work and the protection attached to it.
A near miss is the only free data a system gets. Why they go unreported and how to fix that.
Log one near miss properly and trace what happens to the record.
Fatigue is a hazard with the same standing as a chemical or a height, and is treated as weakness.
Map your own fatigue risk across a real week and identify one controllable factor.
Every workplace has a normalised shortcut. Naming yours and understanding why it persists.
Identify the shortcut, describe the pressure creating it, and propose the fix.
Protective equipment that does not fit is not protective equipment, and fit is a right.
Check the fit of your own equipment against its specification and report the gap.
The hours after an incident: preserving the scene, the record, and your own account.
Write the account you would need to give, from a real or documented incident.
Raising a concern about a colleague, which is the hardest safety act and the most necessary.
Prepare the conversation, name the fact, and separate it from the person.
Being asked to break a rule by somebody with authority over you, and the response prepared in advance.
Write the response you would give, and identify the escalation route if it fails.
VO: Voice at Work
Reading your own contract for the four clauses that will matter, before they matter.
Locate notice, hours, duties and termination in your own contract and summarise each.
Working time, rest breaks, and the difference between what is offered and what is required.
State the legal minimum where you are and compare it to your actual pattern.
Reading a payslip line by line, and what to do when the number is wrong.
Reconcile one payslip against hours worked and the stated rate.
A grievance is a process with steps and timescales, and it works better written than spoken.
Draft a grievance for a real or worked example, following the actual process.
What a union is, what it can and cannot do, and how membership actually functions.
Explain to somebody else what a union does, without slogans in either direction.
When a problem is yours alone and when it is shared, and why that changes the route.
Take one workplace problem and argue both framings.
Discrimination, the categories protected where you are, and the specific route for it.
Identify the route and the time limit that applies where you work.
Disclosure in the public interest: what is protected, what is not, and the order of steps.
Map the internal route and the point at which external disclosure becomes protected.
Redundancy as a process with consultation, selection and entitlement, each contestable.
Calculate the notice and payment owed in a worked example.
Leaving without burning what you built, and what you are entitled to take.
Write a resignation and handover that a former manager would give a reference after.
LD: Lead Practitioner
The shift from doing the work to being accountable for it, and what changes on day one.
Write down what you will stop doing yourself, and tell your team.
Delegating the whole task with the authority attached, and staying available without hovering.
Delegate one real task with a written brief and an agreed check-in.
Preparing a hard conversation so that the fact leads and the judgement follows.
Script the opening two sentences of a real conversation and have them critiqued.
Describing performance in observable behaviour rather than a number, and why the number distorts.
Rewrite one scored assessment as a description of what was observed.
Hiring against a real constraint, and what you can offer when money is not it.
Write the honest pitch for a role you would have to fill.
Noticing that somebody is struggling, and the boundary between support and diagnosis.
Rehearse the opening question, and name the referral you would not attempt yourself.
Enforcing a rule you would not have written, and being honest about that with your team.
Explain one such rule to your team without pretending you agree.
Managing your own manager: what to escalate, when, and in what form.
Write one escalation that gives a decision-maker exactly what a decision needs.
A team after a departure is a different team, and pretending otherwise costs more.
Run a redistribution conversation and publish what changed for whom.
The obligations of the role, and the ones people wrongly assume come with it.
Write the two lists and check them against your organisation’s actual policy.

QU: Research Explorer
The difference between a question that is interesting and one that has a possible answer.
Take a vague question and produce three answerable versions of it.
Reading structure first, methods second, abstract last, and where the real claim sits.
Read one paper this way and summarise the claim and the evidence separately.
Finding what has been tried, including the attempts that were never published.
Produce a prior-work summary that includes at least one unpublished or null result.
Framing so that a result could contradict you, which is the whole point of the exercise.
State your hypothesis and the observation that would falsify it.
Scoping to the study you can actually run with the time, money and access you have.
Cut a proposed study to what your real constraints permit, and name what you lost.
Committing to the analysis before seeing the data, and why that feels like a cost.
Write a preregistration for a small study, including the analysis plan.
Finding disagreement early, when it is cheap, rather than at review, when it is not.
Present your question to somebody likely to object and record their objection.
The literature that undercuts your idea is the most valuable literature you will read.
Find the strongest contrary paper and state what it would take to reconcile.
Stopping before you start, and why that decision is almost never rewarded.
Write the case for not running one study, and the conditions that would change it.
Writing the question first fixes the method to the question rather than the reverse.
Produce a one-page question document dated before any method is chosen.
ME: Method Practitioner
Selecting an instrument for the measurement you need, not the one already on the bench.
Justify an instrument choice against the precision the question requires.
Calibration as a schedule rather than an event, and the drift that hides between them.
Produce a calibration record and identify the drift it would have caught.
Every control rules out one specific alternative explanation. Naming which.
For a real protocol, state what each control eliminates.
Deciding how many before collecting any, and what happens when you decide after.
Perform a sample size calculation and state its assumptions.
Blinding where the design permits it, and being explicit where it does not.
Identify where blinding is possible in your work and where it is not, with reasons.
Recording contemporaneously, because reconstructed records are a different kind of record.
Keep a contemporaneous log for one full procedure.
A deviation from protocol is data about the study; hiding it is data about you.
Log a real deviation with its cause and its likely effect.
Distinguishing contamination, instrument error and a genuine negative result.
Take three anomalous results and classify each with the evidence.
Writing a method somebody else could execute without asking you a question.
Hand your method to somebody who has not seen it and record every question they ask.
When the method constrains the answer, and how to notice that before publication.
Identify one methodological choice in your work that bounds what you could conclude.
DA: Data Practitioner
Raw data is never edited. Everything else is a derived copy with a recorded transformation.
Produce a directory structure that makes overwriting raw data difficult.
Versioning notebooks, protocols, spreadsheets and images, not only code.
Set up and demonstrate versioning for one non-code artefact.
Missingness is information. Recording why a value is absent before deciding what to do.
Classify the missing values in one dataset by cause.
An outlier is a hypothesis about an error until you have investigated it.
Investigate one outlier and document the decision to keep or exclude.
Using the test you can explain, and citing nothing you could not derive the meaning of.
Explain one statistical test you use, in writing, without jargon.
What a p-value is, what it is not, and the four claims routinely made that it cannot support.
Correct four misstatements about p-values from real published text.
Looking at the data before modelling it, because the plot finds what the model assumes away.
Produce the diagnostic plots for one dataset before any model is fitted.
A dataset somebody else can use has a dictionary, units, provenance and a licence.
Publish one small dataset with all four present.
Consent for human data, what it covered, and the analysis it does not permit.
Read one consent form and state an analysis it would not authorise.
Nothing is deleted quietly. Removal is recorded with a reason and a name.
Demonstrate a deletion log for one real removal.
RP: Reproducibility Lead
Somebody replicating your work is treating it as important. Responding accordingly.
Prepare the package a replicator would need, before anyone asks.
Attempting your own result a year later, which is the cheapest reproducibility test there is.
Reproduce one of your own results from your own records alone.
A notebook written for a stranger, because in two years you are the stranger.
Have somebody unfamiliar follow one of your notebook entries.
Capturing the environment as well as the code, since versions decide results.
Produce a runnable environment specification for one analysis.
The result that will not reproduce, and the interval before you know which of you is wrong.
Document a failed reproduction fairly, from both sides.
Publishing a null result, where to publish it, and why it matters to people you will never meet.
Draft a null result write-up to publication standard.
Correcting the record: the mechanisms, their speed, and the reputational arithmetic.
Draft a correction for a real or worked error.
Preprints, peer review, and what each one does and does not certify.
Explain to a non-specialist what peer review does and does not guarantee.
Fraud, error, and the large space between them where most problems actually live.
Classify three documented cases and defend each classification.
Reproducibility has a cost, it falls on somebody, and pretending otherwise is why it does not happen.
Cost the reproducibility work for one project and identify who pays.
CO: Research Citizen
Authorship criteria, applied honestly, including the conversation held before the work starts.
Apply a published authorship standard to a real project and write the order down.
Reviewing is a debt to a system that reviewed you, and it is done properly or not at all.
Write one review to a standard you would be glad to receive.
Explaining your work without condescension and without losing the qualifications that matter.
Explain your work in five minutes to somebody outside the field, and be corrected by them.
Dual use considered at design time, when the design can still change.
Write the dual-use paragraph for your own work, honestly.
Where funding comes from, what it shapes, and what has to be declared.
Trace the funding of one paper and state what it could have influenced.
Declaring interests, including the ones that feel too small to mention.
Write your own declaration and have somebody challenge its completeness.
Mentoring as a structured obligation rather than an ambient goodwill.
Agree a written mentoring arrangement with expectations on both sides.
Leaving research without treating it as a failure, and what transfers.
Map your research skills onto three non-academic roles, specifically.
Advising government: the difference between evidence and a recommendation, and who owns each.
Write a one-page advice note that separates the two explicitly.
Public money, public accountability, and what the public is actually owed.
Produce the plain-language summary that should accompany your work.

MC: Machine Explorer
Counting degrees of freedom on a real mechanism and predicting what it cannot reach.
Count them on a physical rig and demonstrate an unreachable pose.
Forward and inverse kinematics understood by moving something with your hands first.
Predict an end-effector position, then measure it.
What each sensor physically responds to, and the thing it is routinely assumed to sense instead.
For three sensors, state the physical quantity and one common misreading.
Actuators, the force available, and the limits that are structural rather than software.
Identify the limiting component in a real actuator chain.
Power budgets, and why the stated runtime and the observed runtime differ.
Measure actual runtime under load and reconcile it with the specification.
Calibrating a real machine, and the error that calibration cannot remove.
Calibrate a rig and quantify the residual error.
Mechanical failure has an acoustic signature before it has a functional one.
Identify a fault by sound and confirm it by inspection.
Maintenance as a scheduled discipline that prevents the failure rather than diagnosing it.
Produce and follow a maintenance schedule for one machine.
Reading a schematic well enough to find a component you have never seen.
Locate three components on hardware using only the schematic.
Building something that moves, which is where every abstraction gets tested.
Build a mechanism that performs one repeatable motion, and document its limits.
SA: Robot Safety Practitioner
Guarding, interlocks and emergency stops: what each protects and the order they act in.
Trace the stop circuit on a real cell and identify every trigger.
The working envelope, how it is defined, and why standing in it is the recurring incident.
Mark the envelope physically and demonstrate the safe approach.
Speed and separation monitoring, and the assumptions underneath the safe distance.
State the assumptions behind one published separation distance.
A collaborative robot has reduced force, not zero force, and the distinction gets people hurt.
Demonstrate the force limit and state what it does not protect against.
Isolating energy before work, including the stored energy people forget.
Perform a full isolation and identify every stored energy source.
Risk assessment before the first run, written by the people who will operate it.
Produce a risk assessment for a real cell and have an operator challenge it.
A documented case where the safety system did its job, read for what made it work.
Present one case and identify the specific control that held.
A documented case where it did not, read without hindsight bias.
Present one case and identify what was knowable at the time.
Training somebody else on a cell, which is where your own gaps surface.
Train one person and be assessed on their competence, not yours.
The stop you hesitated on, and building the reflex before you need it.
Rehearse the stop until it is automatic, and log the response time.
CT: Control Practitioner
Open loop and closed loop, felt on a real system rather than derived on a board.
Run the same task both ways and measure the difference.
Tuning a system that oscillates, and why the fast solution is usually the wrong one.
Tune a real loop and document each change and its effect.
The sense-plan-act cycle, its timing, and what happens when one stage is late.
Instrument the cycle and find the stage that limits it.
The gap between a plan made in a model and a world that was not in the model.
Run a planned motion in a disturbed environment and record the divergence.
Teleoperation, latency, and the operator behaviours that latency produces.
Operate under induced delay and describe how your own behaviour changed.
Autonomy levels described by what the human must still do, not by marketing.
Classify three real systems by what the human is required to do.
Handover between human and machine, which is where most autonomy incidents occur.
Design and test a handover protocol with an explicit acknowledgement step.
The failure mode you designed for, and proving the design actually handles it.
Induce the anticipated failure and verify the response.
The failure mode you did not, and building the system so it is at least visible.
Identify one unhandled failure and add detection for it.
Logging enough to reconstruct a failure without logging so much that nobody reads it.
Define a logging policy and reconstruct one incident from it alone.
DT: Physical Data Steward
What an episode of robot data actually contains, including what was captured incidentally.
Inventory every stream in one episode, including the unintended ones.
Consent before recording, from everybody in the space and not only the operator.
Produce the consent process for a real workspace recording.

Write the notice a worker in that space is owed, and have one review it.
Designing capture so faces are never recorded, rather than recorded and then removed.
Demonstrate a capture configuration where faces are not acquired at all.
Constraint integrity: a dataset that preserves what was physically impossible in the scene.
Verify that one dataset’s constraints survived its processing pipeline.
Labelling that survives independent review, with the ambiguous cases marked rather than guessed.
Label a sample, have it independently relabelled, and reconcile the disagreements.
Who owns an episode you contributed, and what the licence actually permits.
Read one dataset licence and state what a downstream user may do.
Export, jurisdiction, and where the data physically comes to rest.
Trace one dataset’s path from capture to storage, naming each jurisdiction.
Withdrawal after the fact, and whether the architecture makes it possible at all.
Test a withdrawal request against a real pipeline and report where it fails.
The standard: a dataset you would be content to appear in yourself.
Apply the test to a real dataset and state what would have to change.
WK: Work & Machines Lead
The job before automation and after, described by the person doing it rather than the vendor.
Interview somebody whose work was automated and write their account.
Tasks that should not be automated, and the reasons that are not efficiency reasons.
Argue one such case in your own workplace.
Retraining that starts before the equipment arrives, which is the only time it works.
Draft a retraining timeline anchored to an installation date.
Maintenance as a career rather than a consolation, and what it actually requires.
Map the competencies of a maintenance role and assess yourself against them.
Negotiating automation collectively, and what has historically been won.
Find one real agreement and identify what was secured.
Measuring what changed, including the effects that were not in the business case.
Design the measurement, including one effect the business case omitted.
The skill that became more valuable, and noticing it early enough to invest.
Identify one such skill in your trade and evidence the claim.
The skill that became less valuable, and saying so without pretending otherwise.
Identify one and describe the honest transition from it.
Teaching a machine your trade, and what is lost in the demonstrations.
Record a demonstration set and state what the machine cannot learn from it.
A workshop that adopted machines and kept its people, and the decisions that made that possible.
Present one case and identify the decisions that were not automatic.

PC: Community Health Explorer
The actual scope of the role, and the boundary at which it stops and refers.
State the scope and the referral boundary, and be corrected by a supervisor.
A household visit with a structure, so the same things are covered every time.
Conduct a structured visit under observation and complete the record.
The danger signs that mean refer now, memorised rather than looked up.
Recite the danger signs and demonstrate the referral action for each.
Growth monitoring, the chart, and what a flattening line is telling you.
Plot a real series and identify the point at which action was required.
Immunisation schedules and the cold chain that decides whether the vaccine works.
Check a cold chain record and identify a break.
The three conditions that kill the most children, and what community-level action does.
Demonstrate the assessment and classification for each of the three.
Stock, consumption rates, and forecasting so the resupply arrives before the shortage.
Calculate a resupply quantity from real consumption data.
The register: why it is filled in, who reads it, and what it is not for.
Complete a register correctly and state who sees it and who does not.
Working when the facility is hours away, and what that distance changes.
Map the actual referral time and design around it.
Serving the community you belong to: the trust it buys and the confidentiality it strains.
Describe a real confidentiality conflict and the boundary you would hold.
MN: Maternal & Newborn Practitioner
What antenatal contact is actually for, beyond attendance being counted.
State the purpose of each contact and what it screens for.
Danger signs in pregnancy, recognised and acted on without waiting for confirmation.
Recognise the signs in scenarios and demonstrate the action.
Birth preparedness including the transport plan, which is the part that usually fails.
Complete a birth plan with a named transport arrangement.
The first hour after birth and the small number of things that matter most in it.
Demonstrate the first-hour sequence.
Newborn danger signs, which differ from adult signs and are easily missed.
Identify newborn danger signs in scenarios and state the action.
Postnatal contact, its timing, and the period when most deaths actually occur.
State the schedule and what each visit checks.
Feeding advice that is safe to give at community level, and where it stops.
State what you may advise and what you must refer.
Sitting with loss, without a script that makes it easier for you and harder for them.
Practise the presence, and name what you would not say.
A referral that actually happens: the follow-up that turns advice into arrival.
Track one referral to completion and identify where it nearly failed.
A maternal death review as learning rather than blame, and what it requires of the room.
Participate in a review process and identify one system change it produced.
IN: Infection Practitioner
Hand hygiene as a supplied, timed, monitored system rather than an instruction.
Audit hand hygiene at real moments and report compliance honestly.
Sharps, waste streams, and the injury that happens during disposal rather than use.
Demonstrate safe disposal and state the post-exposure procedure.
The first suspicion of an outbreak, and the cost of waiting for certainty.
Describe the threshold at which you would report, and to whom.
Contact tracing that finds contacts without building a surveillance record.
Design a tracing process and state what it does not retain.
Isolation a household can actually sustain, given one room and shared water.
Design an isolation plan for a real household constraint.
Vaccination where rumour is present, which is answered by relationships, not correction.
Prepare a conversation that starts from the concern rather than the fact.
Protecting the health worker, who is the resource that cannot be resupplied.
Identify your own exposure risks and the controls that exist for each.
Reporting during an outbreak, when the data is worst and matters most.
Complete an outbreak report under time pressure and check it for errors.
When the advice changes, and saying so without destroying the credibility of the next message.
Draft the message explaining a changed instruction.
What the community remembers afterwards, which shapes the next outbreak more than any plan.
Interview somebody about a past outbreak and record what stayed with them.
NC: Long Conditions Practitioner
Hypertension found at home, the measurement, and what community-level follow-up looks like.
Measure correctly, twice, and state the referral threshold.
Diabetes as daily work done by the person, not by the clinic.
Build a daily routine with somebody and identify its failure points.
Why people stop taking medicine, which is rarely the reason assumed.
Interview somebody who stopped and record the actual reasons.
Mental health at community level: what may be supported, and what must be referred.
State the boundary and demonstrate a referral conversation.
Disability and the household around it, including the person doing the caring.
Assess a household’s support need including the carer’s.
Palliative care where there is no hospice, delivered by family with support.
Build a home care plan for comfort, with the family as the deliverer.
Pain relief, the law that restricts it, and the gap that leaves people in.
State the legal position where you are and the route that exists.
The medicine that is out of stock, and what you do in the interval.
Describe the interim plan and the escalation for a real stockout.
A care plan a family can actually run, written in their words.
Write one with a family and have them read it back.
Thirty years of a condition, and what changes across that time.
Map the stages of one long condition and what support each needs.
SY: Health System Citizen
Supervision that develops rather than inspects, and what to ask for from it.
Prepare a supervision session with your own agenda.
Being paid on time as a health worker, and what happens to services when you are not.
Document the payment process and the point at which it breaks.
The referral chain, its breaks, and where a patient is most likely to be lost.
Trace one chain end to end and mark the break points.
Data that goes up and never comes back, and what would change if it did.
Identify one indicator you report and what you would do with it returned.
Working alongside traditional practitioners, who are usually consulted first.
Describe a working relationship that neither dismisses nor endorses.
A ministry, a donor and a project cycle, and how the three shape your work.
Map the funding behind your own role and its end date.
When the project ends: what continues, what stops, and who was told.
Write the honest continuity plan for a project ending.
Career progression for a community health worker, where it exists and where it does not.
Map the available progression where you are, including its absence.
Speaking upward for your community, with evidence rather than anecdote.
Prepare one representation with data and a specific ask.
What you cannot fix, and continuing to work without pretending you can.
Name one, and describe how you hold it.

Rapid assessment that reports its own uncertainty rather than hiding it.

Counting a population in motion, where every method has a known failure.

The data the community already holds, and why it is usually collected again.
Find existing local data and use it rather than duplicating it.
Assessment fatigue: the harm of repeatedly asking people to describe their worst month.
Redesign an assessment to reduce burden and state what you gave up.
Disaggregation that changes a decision, rather than disaggregation as a compliance box.
Disaggregate one dataset and identify a decision it changes.
The gap between what is needed and what is fundable, stated rather than absorbed.
Produce both lists side by side for one context.
Reporting a need smaller than expected, which is professionally harder than the reverse.
Write the finding and the covering note.
Assessing during active conflict, where access bias is the dominant error.

Publishing something that disappoints the organisation that paid for it.

What the cluster system coordinates, and what it does not.

A meeting worth attending, and how to make one, or leave one.

How duplication happens without anybody intending it.

Sharing that somebody is served without sharing anything about them.

Localisation as budget, decision rights and risk transfer, not as vocabulary.

Handover to a national actor, planned from the start rather than at the end.

Consortium bids, who leads, and where the overhead actually lands.
Map the money flow in one consortium structure.
Exit as a designed phase with criteria, not an event triggered by a funding date.

A complaint mechanism people actually use, which is usually not the one that was built.
Test a mechanism from a user’s position and report what stopped you.
Feedback that changes a programme, and the loop that closes back to the person.

Protection from sexual exploitation and abuse: the standards, the reporting, the obligation.

Reporting a colleague, which is the hardest obligation in the sector.
Rehearse the report and identify the protection available to you.
Communicating a decision people will not like, without hiding behind a policy.

Participation that transfers a decision rather than producing a photograph.

Accountability while leaving, which is when it is least convenient and most owed.

Do no harm, examined against a real programme rather than recited.

What people said they wanted, recorded and set beside what was delivered.

Indicators that survive contact with a real context rather than a proposal.
Test three indicators against field reality and revise them.
Cash versus in-kind: the evidence, and the conditions under which each is right.
